claims.claim: DMBOK2 chapter 15, Data Management Maturity Assessment, uses six levels: 0 no capability, 1 initial or ad hoc, 2 repeatable, 3 defined, 4 managed, 5 optimised. It starts at 0, unlike CMM models that start at 1.
claims.source: DAMA-DMBOK2, checked in the printed book by the course owner, 7 November 2026.

claims.claim: The six talent domains (workforce and organisation, recruitment, learning, performance, mobility, skills) come from the role brief, not from DAMA.
claims.source: content/roles/ey-talent.yaml, the job description in the brief.

concept_html:
A maturity baseline records how well each knowledge area is run today, so you can set targets and show progress. DMBOK2 describes a data management maturity assessment. Sources differ on the exact level names, so agree one scale with your stakeholders and write it down. A common version runs from 0 to 5:

  • 0 no capability
  • 1 initial: ad hoc, depends on individuals
  • 2 repeatable: some process, applied unevenly
  • 3 defined: a documented standard, followed across teams
  • 4 managed: measured, with targets and reviews
  • 5 optimised: improved continuously from the measures

Each level builds on the last.

Score a grid, not a single number: knowledge areas down the side, talent domains across the top. A talent platform has six domains: workforce and organisation, recruitment, learning, performance, mobility and skills. Data quality can be at 3 for workforce data and at 1 for skills.

Three rules make a baseline you can defend.

  1. Evidence for every score. A score without a document, a metric or a log is an opinion. "Level 3: quality rules documented in DQ-STD-02 and run nightly" survives a challenge.
  2. Report the weakest area, not the mean. An average of 3 can hide a 0 in data security. One weak area can sink a domain.
  3. Integers only. A level is a stage you have reached. A score of 2.5 says you have not agreed which stage you are at.

The baseline is a snapshot. Rescore at fixed intervals with the same scale, so changes mean progress, not a new yardstick.

exercises.primer:
`isinstance(value, int)` checks a type. In Python, `True` is also an `int`, so check for `bool` first:

```python
isinstance(3, int)       # True
isinstance(2.5, int)     # False
isinstance(True, bool)   # True, and isinstance(True, int) is True too
```

`min` takes a `key` function. A tuple key compares item by item: `min([("b", 1), ("a", 1)], key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0]))` returns `("a", 1)`.

Write `weakest_by_domain(scores: dict[str, dict[str, int]]) -> dict[str, tuple[str, int]]`. `scores` maps each talent domain to a dict of knowledge area to score. Return, for each domain, the weakest area and its score. When two areas tie, pick the one that comes first alphabetically.

Raise `ValueError` if any score is not a whole number from 0 to 5, or if a domain has no scores. A `bool` does not count as a whole number.

Write weakest_by_domain(scores: dict[str, dict[str, int]]) -> dict[str, tuple[str, int]]. scores maps each talent domain to a dict of knowledge area to score. Return, for each domain, the weakest area and its score. When two areas tie, pick the one that comes first alphabetically.

Raise ValueError if any score is not a whole number from 0 to 5, or if a domain has no scores. A bool does not count as a whole number.
solution_lines: MIN_LEVEL = 0
MAX_LEVEL = 5
def weakest_by_domain(scores: dict[str, dict[str, int]]) -> dict[str, tuple[str, int]]:
"""The weakest knowledge area and its score for each talent domain.
Args:
scores: Domain to knowledge area to whole-level score.
Returns:
Domain to (area, score). Ties go to the area first in alphabetical order.
Raises:
ValueError: If a score is not a whole number from 0 to 5, or a domain is empty.
"""
result: dict[str, tuple[str, int]] = {}
for domain, areas in scores.items():
if not areas:
raise ValueError(f"{domain}: no scores")
for area, score in areas.items():
if isinstance(score, bool) or not isinstance(score, int):
raise ValueError(f"{domain}.{area}: score must be a whole number")
if not MIN_LEVEL <= score <= MAX_LEVEL:
raise ValueError(f"{domain}.{area}: score {score} is outside 0 to 5")
result[domain] = min(areas.items(), key=lambda pair: (pair[1], pair[0]))
return result

title: A maturity baseline you can defend
why_html: A firm reported its talent data maturity as 3.1 out of 5 to its board and won budget for an AI pilot. The pilot stalled in week two: nobody owned access to performance data, which scored 0 for data security in the performance domain. The average had hidden it. A grid reporting the weakest area per domain would have put security ahead of the pilot.
